lesson.title: More Molecules, More Room: Avogadro's Law
lesson.summary: Avogadro's law states that at constant temperature and pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to the number of moles present, so equal volumes of any gas under the same conditions contain equal numbers of particles.
lesson.body:
Avogadro's law is the third special case hiding inside PV = nRT, this time obtained by holding temperature and pressure constant instead of the pairs used for Boyle's and Charles's laws. If P, R, and T are fixed, rearranging PV = nRT gives V/n = RT/P, a constant, so V1/n1 = V2/n2. This is a direct relationship, just like Charles's law: add more moles of gas at constant temperature and pressure, and the volume grows right along with it.

This law connects directly to the mole concept in a way that surprised chemists when it was first proposed: Avogadro's law says that the identity of the gas does not matter at all. One mole of helium and one mole of nitrogen, at the same temperature and pressure, occupy exactly the same volume, even though a helium atom and a nitrogen molecule have very different masses and sizes. This makes sense once you remember that gas particles are so far apart that their individual size is negligible compared to the empty space around them; what determines volume is simply how many particles are bouncing around and pushing the walls apart, not what those particles weigh or how big they are.

A worked example: suppose a flexible container holds 3.00 L of gas containing 0.500 mol of particles, at some fixed temperature and pressure. If you pump in more gas until the container holds 1.20 mol total, still at the same temperature and pressure, what is the new volume? Using V1/n1 = V2/n2, rearranged to solve for V2: V2 = V1 times (n2 / n1) = 3.00 L times (1.20 mol / 0.500 mol). The ratio 1.20/0.500 is 2.40, and 3.00 times 2.40 is 7.20 L. The amount of gas more than doubled (from 0.500 to 1.20 mol is a factor of 2.40), and the volume grew by exactly that same factor, from 3.00 L to 7.20 L.

Avogadro's law is the theoretical foundation for molar volume, covered later in this unit, which uses this exact proportionality to state that one mole of any ideal gas occupies the same volume at a given temperature and pressure, a fixed number you can look up and use directly instead of solving PV = nRT from scratch every time.
